questions.q: What is Oracle's default index type, and which SQL Server index does it most resemble in behavior?
options: The B-tree index, which behaves like a SQL Server nonclustered index
The bitmap index, which behaves like a SQL Server columnstore index
The index-organized table, which behaves like a SQL Server heap
Oracle has no default index type; every index must specify its structure explicitly
questions.explain: Oracle's default B-tree index is structurally similar to a SQL Server nonclustered index — a balanced tree suited to high-cardinality columns.

questions.q: What does a plain Oracle table default to, in the absence of a clustered-index equivalent?
options: A heap — an index-organized table (IOT) is the closer analog to a clustered index, but it's a distinct, deliberately chosen table type
Every Oracle table is automatically index-organized by default
Oracle tables cannot store data until a clustered index is created
A bitmap-organized structure by default
questions.explain: Unlike SQL Server, where a clustered index is common, a plain Oracle table is a heap by default; an IOT is available but must be chosen deliberately.

questions.q: Why are bitmap indexes well suited to low-cardinality columns in analytical workloads?
options: They store a bitmap per distinct value, and bitwise AND/OR operations across bitmaps are cheap, which fits multi-condition analytical queries
They store a separate B-tree for every single row, making point lookups instant
They automatically convert to B-tree indexes whenever cardinality is low
They require no storage space at all regardless of table size
questions.explain: A bitmap per distinct value makes combining conditions with AND/OR cheap via bitwise operations, which is exactly the pattern analytical queries use.

questions.q: Why are bitmap indexes generally a poor fit for OLTP tables with frequent concurrent single-row writes?
options: Updating one row can require locking an entire bitmap segment covering many rows, hurting concurrency
Bitmap indexes cannot be created on any table larger than 1,000 rows
Bitmap indexes automatically drop themselves after each transaction
OLTP tables are physically incompatible with any kind of index in Oracle
questions.explain: Because a bitmap segment can cover many rows, a single-row update can force locking that segment, which is harmful under frequent concurrent OLTP writes.

questions.q: What problem does a function-based index solve, such as one built on UPPER(last_name)?
options: It allows the optimizer to use an index for a predicate that wraps a column in a function or expression, which a plain B-tree index on the raw column can't support
It replaces the need for the underlying table's primary key
It automatically uppercases all data stored in the column
It only works with bitmap indexes, never B-tree indexes
questions.explain: A function-based index stores the result of the expression itself, so a predicate matching that expression (like UPPER(last_name) = 'SMITH') can use an index instead of forcing a full scan.
